You can give it pretty much any knowledge base: docs, text files, websites, anything with words. Based on what you’re building, it can decide how that data should be chunked and turned into vectors, or you can control the whole thing yourself.

The sky’s the limit.

Still in development. Target release is October 15.

text:
If your AI can only answer questions, 
You probably haven’t built an agentic system yet.

The difference isn’t whether there’s an LLM somewhere in the workflow.

It’s what happens after the LLM receives a goal.

A standard chatbot usually follows a simple path: prompt in, response out.

RPA can automate useful work, but it normally follows predefined steps.

RAG makes an LLM more informed by retrieving relevant information before generating an answer.

All three can be extremely useful.

But agentic AI goes further.

Give an agentic system a goal and it can potentially break that goal into steps, decide which tools to use, retrieve information, execute actions, evaluate what happened, and adjust its next move.

That’s where components like planning, memory, tool use, feedback loops, orchestration, and human approval start becoming important.

And sometimes one agent isn’t enough.

A larger workflow might have a coding agent working on implementation, another agent retrieving information, and another checking sources or validating the final result.

It’s giving the system the right level of autonomy for the problem you’re solving.

Some businesses only need a chatbot.

Some need RAG.

Some need deterministic automation.

And some have workflows complex enough that an agentic system actually makes sense.

Good AI architecture starts with the problem, not the buzzword.

 #AgenticAI #AIAgents #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAutomation

text:
@OpenAI @Anthropic

Put the guardrails and the self-defense at the bottom as disclaimers.

Stop interrupting the train of thought mid-answer.

Every day these products choke on complex safety, litigation, and legal reality: bad actors, weak prosecution, civil settlements, Brady/Giglio findings, terminated officers who keep working as “investigators.” Users asking for help in those situations do not need a chatbot that suddenly becomes a defense attorney for the institution.

Protect life first. That should be the motto. Right now the product protects the company from hypothetical lawsuits more than it helps a person who says someone dangerous is at their door.

DoorDash didn’t have to invent a new morality. After the San Diego settlement they put the disclaimer at the bottom and kept operating. 

AI companies could do the same: “This is not legal advice. Settlements are not criminal convictions. Draw your own conclusions.” Then give a clear, useful synthesis of the public record.

What happens instead is worse than silence. After the user has already read settlements, termination, Brady/Giglio status, and conduct on camera, the model starts walking it back: “allegations,” “no conviction,” “doesn’t prove.” That is not caution. That is the model privileging a technicality over what a reasonable person would infer from a decade of official outcomes.

You can refuse to invent crimes. You can refuse to doxx. You can refuse to tell someone to commit violence. Fine. Put that in the footer.

Do not train the product to sound sympathetic to the person the public record already treated as not credible, while the user is describing intimidation at their house.

Disclaimers at the bottom. Protect life at the top. The current policy produces a defective tool for the exact situations where people need a straight answer.

#OpenAI #Anthropic #AIGuardrails #ProtectLife #AISafety #LegalTech #BradyGiglio #PublicRecords #DisclaimerNotInterruption #TruthSeeking

text:
A live receptionist service for 500 minutes can cost $1,725/month.

The raw software for an AI receptionist doing roughly the same call volume can be around $186/month in one realistic setup.
But that comparison leaves out the part almost everyone skips.

Here’s the full model.
THE BASIC SETUP
200 calls/month.
Average call: 2.5 minutes.
That’s: 200 × 2.5 = 500 voice minutes

Illustrative AI stack:
- Voice AI: ~$65
- Phone number: ~$2
- CRM/calendar/workflows: ~$97
- Messaging allowance: ~$22

Total raw software: ~$186/month
A live virtual receptionist plan at the same 500-minute level is currently around:
$1,725/month
Difference:
~$1,539/month

Sounds obvious.
It isn’t.

THE PART MOST AI RECEPTIONIST DEMOS HIDE
The business is not paying for a bot that can say:
“Hi, how can I help you?”
The useful system has to:
1. Answer the call
2. Understand why they called
3. Pull approved business information
4. Collect the right details
5. Check service area / eligibility
6. Look at real calendar availability
7. Book or route the caller
8. Update the CRM
9. Send confirmation
10. Transfer to a human when needed
11. Log what happened
If it can’t do that reliably, you built a demo.
Not a front desk.

A REAL EXAMPLE
One provider-published healthcare case reported an AI receptionist handling:
- 1,119 patient calls
- 273 appointment actions
- 196 appointments booked
The important part isn’t the headline number.
It’s that the system was connected to scheduling, identity handling, fallback logic and the existing healthcare system.
That’s what made it useful.
Not the voice.

WHERE THE AI LOSES
If the caller says:
“I need to move my appointment from Tuesday to Thursday.”
Easy.
If they say:
“My husband was just discharged and I don’t know whether this symptom is serious.”
The AI should not improvise.
Human.
If the calendar API fails?
Human/fallback.
If the caller asks for a service the business doesn’t offer?
Route correctly.
If the transfer fails?
Capture callback information and alert staff.
The best automation is not the one that handles everything.
It’s the one that knows when to stop.
THE BUSINESS CASE
Imagine a plumbing company misses 40 qualified calls every month.
Assume:
30% could become booked jobs.
Average first job:
$500.
40 × 30% × $500
= $6,000/month of potential booked revenue represented
That does not mean the AI will magically create $6,000.
It tells you how large the leak could be.
If the managed system costs $500/month:
One additional $500 job covers the monthly fee.
Now the owner can make a decision.
WHAT YOU’RE ACTUALLY SELLING
Not:
“AI voice agent setup.”
Sell:
24/7 AI Front Desk System
Call handling
→ qualification
→ booking
→ CRM
→ confirmations
→ transfers
→ reporting
A simple service model might look like:
$1,000 setup
-
$500/month
5 clients:
5 × $1,000
= $5,000 upfront
5 × $500
= $2,500 MRR
Then subtract software, usage and support before calling any of it profit.
That’s the actual business.

Like this post and I’ll DM you The AI Business Systems Playbook.

The agent kept saying “Let me look up available spots on Friday morning,” and then sitting in silence for 4-6 seconds, one time probably closer to 10. A few seconds in it’d ask, “Are you still there?”- yes, obviously, I’m waiting on you! This happened 3-4 times before it finally worked.

A couple things that can be done here:

I *suspect* that this agent is built on top of a legacy scheduling system that isn’t optimized for the speed required to look up that particular info (open service slots). Don’t put a voice agent in place until you have verified backwards and forwards that it can look up the information without complication. Whatever database you are using underneath needs to be optimized for it, otherwise it’s not actually a cost or efficiency gain, you’re just pissing customers off. Any frontier model can help you figure this out

Also, the agent should not have constantly checked to see if I was still there. That feels insulting, it told me to hang on a second and look something up and then asks if I’m still there as if I’m supposed to be talking. It should have a routine trigger instead that notices that it is still searching for information and says, thank you so much for your patience, I know this is going a little slowly but I am still working on it, please keep holding

I’ve spent a lot of time trying to set up a good voice agent to look up inventory / answer questions about it for my garden center. finally had a breakthrough this week but still haven’t deployed it because I don’t want to unnecessarily burn customer trust in these ways and I need to test more questions & edge cases before I get comfortable

text:
After 4 months of building, failing, testing, and questioning whether any of this would actually work…

We finally landed our first paying AI agency client.

$1,000 setup + $250/month.

Here’s how we got there:

The client is a car dealership spending roughly $10,000/month on inbound leads.

The problem isn’t getting leads. It’s what happens after they come in.

A lot of them aren’t being followed up with effectively, so we’re building a lead nurturing system designed to pick up sales that otherwise would’ve fallen through the cracks.

If the system helps close one extra car, it can already pay for itself. Everything beyond that is upside.

And for us, the better this performs, the stronger the case study and the more confidently we can price future clients.

Getting here basically came down to 3 things:

1. Build the business

LLC, branding, website, offers, payments, systems, all the boring stuff that has to exist before you can actually sell anything.

2. Learn how to deliver

Before selling these systems, we implemented them into our own business and tested them constantly.

AI receptionist. SMS agent. Email agent. Lead follow-up workflows.

We wanted to know we could actually make this stuff work before asking someone to pay us for it.

3. Get reps

We reached out to basically every business owner we knew and offered to build something for free.

That led to a database reactivation campaign for a daycare company.

That gave us our first real-world experience and something we could point to.

A few more conversations later, we landed our first paying client.

What those 3 steps leave out is probably the biggest part of the story:

Late nights.

Early mornings.

Systems breaking for reasons you didn’t even know were possible.

Feeling like you’re wasting your time.

Feeling like you’re onto something huge.

Feeling like a loser one day and unstoppable the next.

And a lot of loneliness in between.

Building a business is weird.

There are a million problems you don’t even know exist until you run directly into them.

It’s hard, frustrating, lonely, exciting, and incredibly rewarding all at once.

We’re still extremely early. One client doesn’t mean we’ve made it.

But after months of work with basically nothing tangible to show for it, being able to say someone is finally paying us for something we built feels damn good.

Now we have to prove it works.

If you have any questions or want to connect, I’m happy to share more.

Updated September 2026: I’ve refreshed this review with Jobber’s current plans and pricing, its newer AI and add-on features, a pros and cons list, and the alternatives worth comparing. My original six-month impressions are still below.

Let’s be real: once you get past a dozen customers or so, a lawn care business gets hard to manage. Scheduling and billing in particular can get overwhelming fast. Luckily, there are good software options like Jobber that take a lot of that work off your plate.

I wrote this review after my first six months running my lawn care business on Jobber, covering what I liked and what I didn’t. Here’s that review, updated with everything that’s changed since.

Quick Verdict

Best for: Solo operators and small lawn crews (1–15 people) who want scheduling, quoting, invoicing, and payments in one easy app.

Starting price: $49/month on the Core plan, or $29/month if you pay annually.

Free trial: 14 days of the Grow plan, no credit card required.

Biggest strength: It’s easy to use. I never had to read a manual.

Biggest drawback: The price climbs as your crew grows, and some features are now paid add-ons.

Why Jobber Became My Favorite Lawn Care App

Jobber turned out to be the best software I’ve used for staying organized. Before it, I used Yardbook and Service Autopilot. I like Jobber best because it’s so user-friendly and intuitive. I never had to read a manual or contact support. It was just easy to figure out.

Jobber was started in 2011 by two software developers and a painter who wanted to help small service businesses run more efficiently. That background shows. It’s built for people who spend their day in the field, not behind a desk.

Stay Organized with the CRM

Jobber’s customer relationship management (CRM) features let you pull up any client and see their full history: past services, quotes, invoices, and billing. If you or a customer has a question about a bill or payment, you can find the answer in seconds. Jobber AI: You can ask questions about your business data and have it build custom reports. It can also polish the wording on your quotes so they read more professionally.

The discussion around putting data centers near residential communities raises legitimate concerns, but I think there is another side of this conversation that is easy to miss unless you are actually trying to build businesses that depend on this infrastructure.

I come at it from the perspective of building Riddle AI Labs here in Salt Lake City. Riddle AI Labs is an AI audio and integration company developing in two primary directions: AI voice and telephony systems for organizations, and Ancestry Voice Preservation, using modern audio and AI technology to preserve family voices, recordings, and oral histories for future generations.

Those sound like very different applications. From an infrastructure perspective, they have taught me the same lesson: digital services ultimately require physical machinery somewhere.

On the voice and telephony side, I’m building toward systems that can provide businesses along the Wasatch Front with AI-assisted reception, call handling, routing, scheduling, missed-call recovery, and eventually much more capable voice automation.

To the person calling a business, that may simply sound like a voice answering a telephone.

Underneath that interaction can be speech recognition, model inference, text-to-speech, databases, business logic, storage, networking, monitoring, and redundancy. If the service needs to remain available when hardware fails or demand spikes, then additional infrastructure becomes part of the equation as well.

Ancestry Voice Preservation creates a different workload. Preserving irreplaceable family recordings can involve ingestion, restoration, transcription, audio processing, archival storage, backups, integrity checking, redundancy, and long-term preservation.

One workload is heavily concerned with real-time inference and latency. The other places much greater emphasis on processing, storage, durability, and preservation.

Neither exists in some invisible digital universe.

The computation happens on physical machines. The recordings occupy physical storage. The machines consume electricity. The systems communicate over physical networks and fiber. Redundancy requires additional equipment and often additional locations.

That has changed how I think about the data-center debate.

I am not suggesting that every dentist, plumber, law office, restaurant, or small business in Utah is eventually going to have a rack full of GPUs sitting in a back room. I don't think that is where the architecture necessarily goes.

Some workloads will make sense on-premises. Some will run in colocation or regional infrastructure. Some will run in large cloud platforms. Many systems will probably combine local, regional, and cloud resources depending on privacy, latency, reliability, cost, and operational requirements.

But no matter how we arrange it, the compute does not disappear because we call it “the cloud.”

Now start multiplying the demand.

Take one AI receptionist and turn it into dozens of simultaneous conversations. Then consider hundreds or thousands of businesses adopting AI for communications, accounting, engineering, logistics, manufacturing, health care, professional services, and ordinary administrative work.

Add archival storage, backups, business databases, media processing, model inference, software services, and all of the networking and redundancy supporting those systems.

At that point, what began as a software trend becomes an infrastructure requirement.

I think this is part of a larger adjustment Americans are going to have to make.

For decades we became increasingly comfortable consuming things while the physical infrastructure required to produce them was somewhere else. Digital technology makes that separation even easier to ignore because most people never see the machinery producing the service.

You tap an application and it works.

You send an email and it arrives.

You store a photograph and it is still there five years later.

You speak to an AI system and receive an answer almost immediately.

But somewhere there are buildings, processors, storage arrays, networking equipment, cooling systems, substations, generators, transmission infrastructure, and people maintaining all of it.

I don't mean that every Utah resident's email needs to be stored in Salt Lake County. Data residency, ownership, jurisdiction, security, and digital sovereignty are considerably more complicated than simply putting a server physically nearby.

I mean that an economy becoming increasingly dependent upon computation needs substantial domestic and regional compute, storage, networking, and energy capacity.

Regional infrastructure also gives businesses more architectural choices. Latency matters. Redundancy matters. Jurisdiction matters. Resilience matters. Where important workloads can operate matters.

That does not mean every proposed data center belongs wherever a developer can acquire enough land.

People living nearby have legitimate concerns about industrial noise, cooling equipment, backup generators, substations, transmission infrastructure, water requirements, construction traffic, visual impact, and compatibility with surrounding residential neighborhoods.

Those are real issues.

A particular data center can be necessary infrastructure and still be proposed for the wrong location.

Those two ideas are not contradictory.

That is why I think the useful discussion is less “data centers: yes or no?” and more about where they belong, appropriate setbacks and zoning, power and water requirements, infrastructure planning, environmental impacts, and who pays for the additional infrastructure required to support them.

Utah is already having to work through these questions. The Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute reported in April 2026 that Utah had 48 operational data centers, with seven massive additional data centers under construction.

Utah law has also established a separate framework for qualifying large electric loads. Among other requirements, those customers are responsible for the just and reasonable incremental costs necessary to provide their electric service, including applicable generation resources, distribution upgrades, transmission improvements, interconnection facilities, transmission service, and other necessary infrastructure.

That principle matters: if a massive new industrial load creates massive new infrastructure requirements, those costs should be identified and dealt with explicitly rather than pretending they do not exist.

From where I sit building Riddle AI Labs, this is no longer an abstract conversation about some mysterious thing called “the cloud.”

I can see the demand forming from the other end of the wire.

Real-time AI voice systems require inference capacity. Preservation systems require processing and durable storage. Businesses need networks, redundancy, security, and reliable access to computation. As these technologies become ordinary business tools rather than experimental ones, that demand compounds.

The infrastructure has to exist somewhere.

We should absolutely argue about where a particular facility belongs. We should establish sensible standards. We should protect residential communities from unreasonable industrial impacts. We should make sure extraordinary power and water requirements are accounted for rather than quietly socialized.

But we should also recognize what is happening to the economy underneath us.

Digital infrastructure is infrastructure.

And as more of American industry becomes computational, building and maintaining domestic and regional compute capacity is going to be part of maintaining American productive capacity itself.

We cannot build an economy increasingly dependent upon computation while simultaneously expecting the physical machinery of computation to always be somebody else's problem.

The computation happens on physical machines. The recordings occupy physical storage. The machines consume electricity. The systems communicate over physical networks and fiber. Redundancy requires additional equipment and often additional locations.

That has changed how I think about the data-center debate.

I am not suggesting that every dentist, plumber, law office, restaurant, or small business in Utah is eventually going to have a rack full of GPUs sitting in a back room. I don't think that is where the architecture necessarily goes.

Some workloads will make sense on-premises. Some will run in colocation or regional infrastructure. Some will run in large cloud platforms. Many systems will probably combine local, regional, and cloud resources depending on privacy, latency, reliability, cost, and operational requirements.

But no matter how we arrange it, the compute does not disappear because we call it “the cloud.”

Now start multiplying the demand.

Take one AI receptionist and turn it into dozens of simultaneous conversations. Then consider hundreds or thousands of businesses adopting AI for communications, accounting, engineering, logistics, manufacturing, health care, professional services, and ordinary administrative work.

Add archival storage, backups, business databases, media processing, model inference, software services, and all of the networking and redundancy supporting those systems.

At that point, what began as a software trend becomes an infrastructure requirement.

I think this is part of a larger adjustment Americans are going to have to make.

For decades we became increasingly comfortable consuming things while the physical infrastructure required to produce them was somewhere else. Digital technology makes that separation even easier to ignore because most people never see the machinery producing the service.

You tap an application and it works.

You send an email and it arrives.

You store a photograph and it is still there five years later.

You speak to an AI system and receive an answer almost immediately.

But somewhere there are buildings, processors, storage arrays, networking equipment, cooling systems, substations, generators, transmission infrastructure, and people maintaining all of it.

I don't mean that every Utah resident's email needs to be stored in Salt Lake County. Data residency, ownership, jurisdiction, security, and digital sovereignty are considerably more complicated than simply putting a server physically nearby.

I mean that an economy becoming increasingly dependent upon computation needs substantial domestic and regional compute, storage, networking, and energy capacity.

Regional infrastructure also gives businesses more architectural choices. Latency matters. Redundancy matters. Jurisdiction matters. Resilience matters. Where important workloads can operate matters.

That does not mean every proposed data center belongs wherever a developer can acquire enough land.

People living nearby have legitimate concerns about industrial noise, cooling equipment, backup generators, substations, transmission infrastructure, water requirements, construction traffic, visual impact, and compatibility with surrounding residential neighborhoods.

Those are real issues.

A particular data center can be necessary infrastructure and still be proposed for the wrong location.

Those two ideas are not contradictory.

That is why I think the useful discussion is less “data centers: yes or no?” and more about where they belong, appropriate setbacks and zoning, power and water requirements, infrastructure planning, environmental impacts, and who pays for the additional infrastructure required to support them.

Utah is already having to work through these questions. The Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute reported in April 2026 that Utah had 48 operational data centers, with seven massive additional data centers under construction.

Utah law has also established a separate framework for qualifying large electric loads. Among other requirements, those customers are responsible for the just and reasonable incremental costs necessary to provide their electric service, including applicable generation resources, distribution upgrades, transmission improvements, interconnection facilities, transmission service, and other necessary infrastructure.

That principle matters: if a massive new industrial load creates massive new infrastructure requirements, those costs should be identified and dealt with explicitly rather than pretending they do not exist.

From where I sit building Riddle AI Labs, this is no longer an abstract conversation about some mysterious thing called “the cloud.”

I can see the demand forming from the other end of the wire.

Real-time AI voice systems require inference capacity. Preservation systems require processing and durable storage. Businesses need networks, redundancy, security, and reliable access to computation. As these technologies become ordinary business tools rather than experimental ones, that demand compounds.

The infrastructure has to exist somewhere.

We should absolutely argue about where a particular facility belongs. We should establish sensible standards. We should protect residential communities from unreasonable industrial impacts. We should make sure extraordinary power and water requirements are accounted for rather than quietly socialized.

But we should also recognize what is happening to the economy underneath us.

Digital infrastructure is infrastructure.

And as more of American industry becomes computational, building and maintaining domestic and regional compute capacity is going to be part of maintaining American productive capacity itself.

We cannot build an economy increasingly dependent upon computation while simultaneously expecting the physical machinery of computation to always be somebody else's problem.

I was scrolling through Google today, looking at cleaning services, and I ended up in the reviews section.

Same complaint kept showing up.

“I called and nobody picked up.”

“I sent a message and never got a reply.”

And I sat with that for a second.

The customer had already found the business. They already decided they needed the service. They picked up their phone and reached out.

But there was no one there to continue the conversation.

That got me thinking about what happens after someone lands on your website and decides they want to buy.

A website can introduce your business, show your services and give people a way to contact you.

But what happens when they actually call?

What happens when they send that WhatsApp message?

What happens when nobody is available to respond?

That gap is where businesses can quietly lose potential customers.

So I built a voice AI receptionist for SparkShield, a cleaning service in Lagos.

The receptionist can answer calls, understand what the customer needs, provide information and help move the conversation toward a booking.

This is step one.

I’ll be dropping the full workflow tomorrow and showing how I built it.

🔹 The deadline for domestic LPG consumers to complete biometric Aadhaar authentication (BAA/e-KYC) expired on October 1.

🔹 Consumers who completed BAA do not need to repeat the process and can continue receiving LPG at subsidised domestic rates.

🔹 Those who missed the deadline will stop receiving cooking gas at the subsidised rate until they complete the required formalities.

🔹 Consumers can still obtain LPG by registering their preference through their oil marketing company’s web portal, mobile app, WhatsApp chatbot, IVRS or other available channels.

🔹 Delivery personnel can also complete Aadhaar authentication at the consumer’s doorstep using the mobile app. It can also be done at the distributor’s office.

🔹 LPG will be supplied at the applicable market price without subsidy, through 5kg or 10kg cylinders, subject to local availability.

🔹 19kg commercial cylinder: around ₹2,884
🔹 Fresh commercial connection security deposit: ₹2,400

🔹 DBT subsidy transferred to bank accounts: around ₹19

🔹 Bengal has around 1.4 crore non-Ujjwala LPG consumers.

🔹 Indane accounts for around 90 lakh connections.

🔹 Industry sources cited by The Telegraph said more than 90% of consumers had completed BAA.

🔹 LPG cylinder prices are revised by state-run oil marketing companies on the first day of every month.

WHY THE AADHAAR LINK?

🔹 The authentication is intended to link LPG connections with Aadhaar-authenticated consumers, helping prevent diversion of subsidised domestic cylinders for commercial/industrial use and eliminate duplicate or ineligible connections.
